newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German economy gaining, ready for EMU - Kohl.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German economy gaining, ready for EMU - Kohl.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday that the German economic recovery was gathering pace and Bonn would fulfil the convergence criteria to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"For me it is clear: Germany will fulfil the criteria. The euro will come at the agreed time," Kohl told Bonn journalists at his twice-yearly news conference.
Kohl said the German economy was picking up speed and stuck by the official forecast of 2-1/2 percent growth this year. He said output could rise by as much as three percent in 1998.

"The main motor is exports. There are the first signs that the domestic economy is gaining momentum," he said, using a more cautious form of words than in his prepared remarks released before the news conference.

Separately, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in Munich that Bonn would manage to cut its budget deficit this year to three percent of gross domestic product -- the Maastricht treaty limit -- despite pressures on the budget.
That view was disputed by the independent IWH economic research institute.
"Based on the current trends, I find 3.0 percent hard to imagine," IWH president Ruediger Pohl told Reuters in an interview in the east German town of Halle.
Pohl said, however, that a deficit of 3.4 percent of GDP should be no obstacle to Germany joining EMU at its planned start in 1999.
Kohl also urged the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to reach a compromise over government tax reforms, saying a deal could be reached quickly in parliamentary mediation.

Waigel's package of 30 billion marks ($16.7 billion) in income and corporate tax cuts was thrown out of the upper house of parliament earlier this month by the SPD majority, condemning it to a tortuous path through legislative mediation.

"It now depends on the SPD majority in the mediation committee whether the tax reform can take effect as planned," he said. "We, the coalition, are ready to compromise. But we are not willing to give up on key elements of the tax reform."
Kohl said SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine's refusal to do a deal on tax amounted to "treason against the unemployed".
He added that voters would reject the blocking strategy of the SPD and punish the opposition party at next year's general election.
"The voters will see through the tactics of the SPD. They know there is no alternative to our reform course," Kohl said.
"I am ready to make this argument a central theme of the election campaign. The coalition stands for modernisation and progress, the SPD embodies old thinking and immobility."

Kohl sought to quell criticism by some coalition politicians of an earlier deal to cut the solidarity surcharge -- raised to finance the rebuilding of eastern Germany -- by two percentage points to 5.5 percent.
"The reduction of the solidarity surcharge from January 1998 has been agreed by the coalition," he said.
